lesson.title: Climbing the Stairs: Step Functions
lesson.summary: Step functions are piecewise functions built entirely from constant pieces, producing a staircase graph that jumps at each boundary.
lesson.body:
A step function is a special kind of piecewise function in which every single piece is a constant, a flat horizontal segment, rather than a line with slope or a curve. Graphed together, those flat segments stack up like a staircase, jumping straight up or down to the next constant value each time the input crosses a boundary, which is exactly where the name comes from.

Parking garages are a natural setting for step functions, because they typically charge by the hour but round every partial hour up to a full one. Suppose a garage charges 4 dollars for each hour or any part of an hour that a car is parked, for a maximum stay of 5 hours. Then the cost function looks like this: C(h) = 4 for 0 < h <= 1, C(h) = 8 for 1 < h <= 2, C(h) = 12 for 2 < h <= 3, and C(h) = 16 for 3 < h <= 4, with each step exactly 4 dollars higher than the last.

Evaluating this function means locating which interval the input falls into, not doing arithmetic with a formula. A customer parked for 1.5 hours falls into the interval 1 < h <= 2, so C(1.5) = 8 dollars, even though 1.5 is much closer to 1 than to 2. A customer parked for 3.9 hours falls into 3 < h <= 4, so C(3.9) = 16 dollars, the same charge as someone parked for exactly 4 hours, because both fall in the same bracket.

On a graph, each piece of a step function is drawn as a short horizontal segment, and the segments do not connect to each other: at every boundary, the graph jumps straight up to the next level, leaving a visible break. That makes a step function the opposite of a continuous function in the clearest possible way, since you cannot trace it with a pencil without lifting up at every single boundary, and it also makes it discrete in spirit even though the input h can technically be any real number of hours, because the output only ever takes on a small set of separated values.

On a written graph, each horizontal segment of a step function typically ends with a solid dot on one side and an open circle on the other, showing precisely which endpoint belongs to that piece. In the parking example, the segment for C(h) = 8 covers 1 < h <= 2, so it would be drawn with an open circle at h = 1, since h = 1 itself belongs to the lower step, and a solid dot at h = 2, since h = 2 is included in this piece. Reading those endpoint markers correctly is essential, because it tells you which step to use for an input that lands exactly on a boundary.

The most famous step function in mathematics is the floor function, written f(x) = floor(x), which rounds any input down to the nearest integer: floor(2.7) = 2, and floor(3.0) = 3. Whether the context is parking fees, postage rates, or tax brackets, step functions all share this same staircase structure, a sequence of constant pieces from the piecewise family, jumping to a new flat level every time a threshold is crossed.
